cards.title: Cold Email Structure: Deliver Opener and Value in One Message
cards.summary: Unlike DMs, cold email must combine a personal, important-looking subject line and a personable body with a single easy-to-accept value offer in one send.
cards.use_when: Writing the first cold email to a brand, supplier or wholesale partner you want to stock your products or collaborate with.
steps: Treat email as compact — you do not get a separate opener message and later value message, so send both at once.
Make the outside look important and worth opening: a curiosity-based subject line including the recipient's first name so it reads personal rather than spam.
Write the inside as personal and personable, not a dry robotic pitch.
End with one strong value offer that is easy to say yes to — a short video, a free asset, a small low-risk first order — so the reply requires almost no effort.
Warm the sending domain gradually over a long period rather than blasting volume immediately, so future emails don't land in spam.
caveats: Framed for service outreach in the source; the structure transfers to supplier, affiliate and wholesale-partner emails, but the value offer must be something the other party actually wants.

cards.title: Different Is Better Than Better in Outreach Emails
cards.summary: Everyone in a prospect's inbox sends the same dry claim-and-guarantee pitch, so being different and witty wins over being marginally better.
cards.use_when: Designing the angle and creative format for cold email to a brand or retailer when your pitch looks identical to every competitor's.
steps: Study the standard pitch in your space — typically a dry claim about views, revenue or a conditional guarantee — and treat that as the boring baseline you must not match.
Build the angle around your specific DNA, experience and stories rather than generic claims, since you are the one-of-one element no competitor can copy.
Use pattern-breaking creative devices: a small personalized graphic, a witty line, a funny image, or a Loom video email as the value vehicle.
Keep the underlying principles intact (personalization, justification for claims, easy reply CTA) — different is only better when the substance holds up.
caveats: The presenter's strong opinion for cold outreach; he says it only works alongside the other principles taught. The same creative move can miss with a different niche or personality — some recipients find witty, others find it dumb.

cards.title: Borrowed Authority Email: Make an Established Brand the Proof
cards.summary: Point at a top player in the prospect's niche already doing what you recommend, and position yourself as the route to matching them instead of asking for trust.
cards.use_when: Writing a mid-sequence outreach email or PDP, email and funnel critique to a store owner who has no reason yet to trust your recommendations.
steps: Identify a brand in the prospect's own vertical that is visibly ahead and that they already recognize as an authority.
State the gap concretely: what their page, emails or funnel do now versus what the top player's version does.
Frame the recommendation as copying a known winner rather than your personal opinion — the same systems used by that top player.
Give a short low-friction CTA: a recorded walkthrough or a sample asset they can review.
Keep it shorter and straighter than a witty anti-pitch email — borrowed authority is a proof angle, so it does not need jokes.
caveats: Use a relevant, genuinely comparable authority figure; if the example is not someone the prospect respects or recognizes, the borrowed trust never lands.

cards.title: Straight-to-the-Point Outreach Email With Permission to Say No
cards.summary: A three-to-six line email that respects the buyer's time, adds risk reversal and explicitly frees them to decline, lowering pressure and often raising replies.
cards.use_when: Your prospect is busy or senior, or you want a no-frills variant in an outreach sequence for a wholesale, partnership or affiliate pitch.
steps: Open with an explicit time-respect line like 'I value your time so I'll get straight to the point'.
State what you made and its time cost to the recipient: a Loom video or short walkthrough, roughly three minutes.
Say what it will do for them in outcome terms — more conversions from the same traffic, more revenue with zero extra work.
Add risk reversal so saying yes costs them nothing.
Close with a micro-commitment and pressure release: reply yes and you'll send it; if not, that's cool too, just let me know.
Skip wit and jokes in this variant — it is the straight version for buyers who respond to brevity.
caveats: Not a universal winner; the source presents it as one angle among several because different owners respond to different tones.

cards.title: Breakup Email: Create Scarcity With the Last Message
cards.summary: A follow-up framed as the final email that says you are about to delete the asset you made for them; the source reports this format generates very high reply volume.
cards.use_when: A prospect has gone cold after several outreach emails and you are choosing the final follow-up before stopping.
steps: Acknowledge directly that they've gone cold and this is the last email on the subject.
State a concrete, near-term consequence to the asset: you'll take the Loom video down shortly after sending this.
Remind them what the asset covers — for example improvements to their headline or funnel that should lift conversions.
Give one frictionless reply instruction: reply yes and it's sent over.
Keep the tone gracious rather than needy: if not, wish them luck.
caveats: The source calls this the strongest reply-getting follow-up but the claim is anecdotal; the threat must stay plausible — delete an asset you genuinely would remove — or it reads as a bluff.

cards.title: Follow-Up Is the Neglected Half of Outreach
cards.summary: The source argues follow-up matters as much as or more than initial outreach, and that inconsistent, un-followed-up outreach is why people conclude outreach doesn't work.
cards.use_when: Scheduling your outreach cadence and deciding how many touches a brand, supplier or partner should receive before you stop.
steps: Treat follow-up as a designed part of the sequence, not an optional add-on: plan multiple touches over time.
Come back from different angles each time — a new proof point, a different creative format, different offer framing — rather than repeating the same message.
If a prospect replied at any point, do not let them go; a reply proves they are open to the offer once timing is right.
Push discipline over cleverness: the failure mode is people completing steps only partially and then blaming outreach.
Accept that first attempts feel clunky and may not convert immediately; the fix is completing the sequence and improving, not switching methods.
caveats: The presenter states this forcefully from his own agency experience; no numeric reply rates are established, so treat the intensity as opinion, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Video Intro Outreach: Send Video or Voice Note Instead of Text
cards.summary: Stand out from text-only outreach by sending a short video introducing yourself on camera, saying how you help, and offering either a call or free value.
cards.use_when: Instagram or social DM outreach to a brand or store owner when most competitors send plain-text pitches, or when a text pitch has gone unanswered.
steps: Open with a normal warm, specific opener as you would for a text message.
Instead of writing out the value pitch, record a short video or voice note introducing who you are, what you do and how you can help.

End the video either with the call (if that's something you'd be open to, let me know and we can hop on a call) or with the value (a longer walkthrough or sample email sequence — say the word and it's in your inbox in minutes).
Put their name on the video thumbnail or first frame so they see it was made for them specifically.
Look presentable and speak articulately — the source says on-camera competence is itself the authority signal.
Keep the script extremely simple; the presenter says his own script feels too simple to work and still gets results.
caveats: Voice notes work but are stated to be less effective than video. The presenter warns this exact script has been widely shared, so copying it verbatim removes the differentiation — change it and make it your own.

cards.title: Loom Funnel Audit as an Outreach Value Offer
cards.summary: Walk the prospect's own funnel as a customer would, record a sub-four-minute Loom of concrete improvements plus proof for each claim, and offer it as the outreach asset.
cards.use_when: Cold outreach to an ecommerce brand where you can review their product page, landing page, email sequence or funnel for real improvement opportunities.
steps: Go through the prospect's funnel exactly as a customer would — landing/opt-in page, sales page copy, email sequence and email copy — and note where leads could slip.
Record a Loom under four minutes; the presenter suggests roughly three as a practical max.
Give an alternative for each problem, not just a critique, to demonstrate you are providing value.
Justify every claim inside the video — say why a change will help and show the evidence rather than asserting it would be better.
Use a compliment sandwich: lead with what they did well and show you recognize them as the expert, give one or two critiques, close on their strengths.
Reference your own past client results so recommendations carry weight beyond assertion.
Turn on the webcam bubble so they see a face tied to the audit.
caveats: The length is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark; you can edit the recording rather than nailing it in one take.

cards.title: Free Value Assets to Attach to Outreach: Email Sequence, Sales Page Sample, Funnel Audit
cards.summary: Three concrete assets you can hand a prospect up front — a written email sequence, a sample sales page document, or a Loom funnel audit — each doubling as proof of ability.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to attach to cold outreach to a store or brand, especially when the concern is whether you can match their voice.
steps: Free email sequence: write a three-email sequence matching their voice. This directly answers the biggest objection — whether you can sound like them — and if the emails are good they may use them, making you the writer going forward.
Free sales page example: produce a document showing what their sales page copy would look like if you wrote it, so they evaluate actual copy rather than a description of your service.
Loom funnel audit: record a walkthrough of their funnel with alternatives and proof behind each claim.
Combine assets when useful — the presenter sometimes writes a free sales page and records a Loom contrasting their current page with the rewrite.

Before choosing the asset, listen to what the prospect asks for; in the case study the prospect himself listed sequences he needed (ticket sales, upsell, welcome/nurture, revival), which made the follow-up easy to scope.
caveats: These are the presenter's own case examples from his practice; they show what worked for him, not guaranteed results. The work is free up front — you only convert if the quality holds.

cards.title: Answering Budget and Trust Objections With a Low-Risk First Project
cards.summary: Agree with the objection first, then shrink to a small paid test project so the buyer can judge your work without a large commitment.
cards.use_when: A store or brand says your quoted price is over budget or that they won't commit big without seeing your quality — common on retainer or full-funnel quotes.
steps: Agree with the objection immediately (totally understandable — that's a big commitment without seeing what I can do); never argue the deal is already good value, since that creates friction.
Reframe yourself as the one qualifying the fit: see if we're a good fit to work together, not let me show you how good I am.

Propose a single small low-risk project with a concrete deliverable and price — in the case study, one eight-email sequence for $400 when the prospect balked at a 50–60 email project. Treat this as a big-fish-on-the-rod move to expand from, not a market rate.
Once working, keep scope discussion going through their actual needs list so you can price by volume with a discount structure if it makes sense.
Set clear per-unit pricing when volume is large (case study: $150/email standard, reduced to $100/email at volume) so the comparison is legible.
caveats: All dollar figures are this presenter's case study and not benchmarks. He states he can't script every negotiation because each differs — use the pattern (agree, de-risk, reduce scope), not the numbers.

cards.title: Circle Back After a Decline: 'We Already Have Someone' Is a Win
cards.summary: A decline, including 'we already have someone', is worth reusing: people move roles, and the replacement needs a provider, so follow up months later around their next launch.
cards.use_when: A store or brand turns down your outreach or says they already have someone handling product copy, SEO or email.
steps: Read 'we already have somebody for that' as a good signal — they engaged, which means they are open to your type of offer.
Do not push back on the decline; let them know to reach out if that changes.
Track them and re-approach roughly one, two, three months later — people change positions within a year and the replacement usually needs a provider.
Anchor the re-approach to something current and observable: a new product launch, promotion or marketing channel they just started (I saw you recently launched X).
Make a light, low-commitment CTA around that new activity: free value against their new product or a short call about the new channel.
Stay top of mind so when the need appears you are the obvious choice.
caveats: The presenter describes this from his experience as a business owner and says most people misread the decline as a loss; the timeline is his observed pattern, not a guaranteed outcome.

cards.title: Anti-Spam Outreach: Personalize Every Message
cards.summary: An outreach message that announces it is bot-blasted, gets the niche wrong and uses no personalization actively repels the prospect and gets remembered as spam.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own outreach before sending, or designing a scalable outreach process and tempted to automate the messaging.
steps: Check recipient fit: the source's bad example pitched email marketing to a non-fitness prospect while claiming a fitness niche — mismatched targeting wastes everyone's time.

Do not tell the prospect you are spamming: the bad example said it was sending thousands of cold DMs and had no time for warm ones — the source argues that self-disqualifies you from fulfilling the work.
Cut volume-first language like I have 70 prepared emails, hopefully you need email marketing — it communicates you haven't looked at them.
Personalize with something only a real reader would know: reply to their recent story content, reference a specific post, or ask a specific question about their funnel.
Before sending, ask whether the recipient would read it and think this is exactly what I need; if not, rewrite the angle.
caveats: Presented as what-not-to-do from an actual DM received; the lesson is about personalization, not about banning automation tooling itself.

cards.title: Set Up Your Public Profile So the Prospect Pitches You
cards.summary: A profile showing what you do and who you've helped can turn a bare opener into the prospect asking to buy before you ever pitch.
cards.use_when: Preparing your social profile or storefront-facing bio before starting DM outreach, so the opener does the minimum and the profile carries the pitch.
steps: Define your bio around three things: what you do, how you do it, and who you've helped before.
Keep the opener minimal — the case study opener was just a general compliment (love the real estate and wealth gems), which the presenter admits wasn't specific.
Let the profile carry the pitch: in that case the prospect replied asking about email copy pricing without the sender ever mentioning copywriting.
Note the counterpoint: the presenter says he would write a better, more specific opener if repeating it — the profile covers the gap, but a specific opener is still stronger.
Apply the same principle to your storefront equivalents — profile, pinned content, public portfolio links — since they are legible the moment someone checks who messaged them.
caveats: The source example is personal-brand DM outreach, not ecommerce; the transferable part is making your public profile a proof asset, not the exact bio.

cards.title: Pick One Outreach Method and Stick With It
cards.summary: The source argues there is no secret outreach method; the winning method is the one you actually stick with, and advice-seeking questions usually substitute for doing the work.
cards.use_when: Choosing which outreach channel to commit to for wholesale, partnership or affiliate outreach, and tempted to keep researching alternatives.
steps: Pick one known method — cold email, video intro DM, Loom funnel audit — and run it consistently rather than swapping after a few attempts.
Expect first attempts to feel clunky and not land immediately; that is learning the skill, not evidence the method is broken.
When tempted to hunt for an advanced or secret method, redirect that time into improving the value you send.
Remember most competitors never finish the steps at all — the field of people who execute is far smaller than the field who talk about it.
Build copywriting skill and outreach skill at the same time, since each improves the other's output.
Give it weeks or months of consistent execution; the presenter frames the timeline loosely and explicitly says short-term luck is mitigated by long-term volume.
caveats: The presenter's strongly stated opinion, including his claim that no secret method exists. Treat the timeline (a couple weeks, maybe a couple months) as his experience, not a promise.

cards.title: Steal the Ideas, Not the Words, from Outreach Templates
cards.summary: Copy-pasting outreach templates word for word gets recognized instantly; change the phrasing drastically so your message doesn't look like something the prospect has already seen.
cards.use_when: Using any outreach template or swipe file for ecommerce brand, supplier or partner outreach before sending it.
steps: Make a personal copy of every template file you use — in Google Drive use File > Make a copy rather than requesting access — so your edits stay yours.
Treat the template's structure (opener, proof, value offer, CTA, permission to decline) as the reusable part.
Rewrite the words: change the phrasing, the specific reference, the joke and the deliverable so it reads as written for this recipient.
Recognize that widely shared templates circulate to the same prospects; a verbatim send signals you're a beginner and makes the prospect unwilling to work with you.

Keep the specificity check: a line that works for a sales coach (I've been watching your sales advice, it helped me close a deal) is wrong for a fitness or dating coach — the idea travels, the words don't.
caveats: The presenter shares many templates himself and acknowledges that even with volume, duplication is likely; the fix is deliberate rewriting, not template avoidance.

cards.title: Retell the Story, Don't Relive It: Story Email Structure
cards.summary: For story-driven emails, open with the result, relate the problem, bridge the gap and close on the dream state — and write scenes the reader can relive rather than a summary retold.
cards.use_when: Writing a customer story, founder story or testimonial email for a store's list, or critiquing a brand's email sequences for a funnel audit.
steps: Start with the what's-in-it-for-me: lead with the big result up front — six months later she was doing $125k launching and working fewer hours, here's how.
Go back to the problem and agitate it, moving through: problem, who the person is, where they are now, the bridge (how they got there), then the dream state at the end.
Give the reader a CTA at the end pointing to more information.

Write to relive rather than retell: instead of 'I was working long hours for low pay with no promotion, so I started a business', write the scene — one day I worked hard labour until my back throbbed; I was 20 but felt 59; the boss said work harder; that's when I started my business.
Use a structured checklist for your own story emails so critique and writing stay organized, and note precise line-level changes rather than general praise.
caveats: The $125k example is a client's case study, not a promise. The structure is the transferable part; do not fabricate testimonial results to fit the shape.

cards.title: Loom Audit Delivery: Compliment Sandwich and Justified Critiques
cards.summary: In a funnel-audit video, compliment first, critique with proof, and justify every change by referencing past results or a borrowed authority rather than asserting your judgment.
cards.use_when: Recording a value Loom for a store's sales page, product page, email sequence or automation flow, or walking them through a proposed test.
steps: Lead with what they did well and show you recognize them as the expert, so the critique doesn't read as an attack.
Give one or two concrete critiques, each paired with an alternative version and a justification for why it would help.
Reference your own past results or a known authority running the same strategy so the claim rests on more than your assertion.
Show evidence on screen where possible — for example the prospect's emails landing in the promotions tab — before explaining the deliverability implication and the fix.
Close on their strengths again so the video stays constructive.
Keep the recording structured; the presenter uses a written resource during the Loom so the delivery is organized rather than hesitant, and edits the take afterwards.
caveats: Length and structure are presenter heuristics; he sometimes runs longer deliberately to give more options, but states around three minutes as the target.

cards.title: Describe Your Work With a Unique Frame, Not a Crowded Label
cards.summary: The presenter avoids calling himself a copywriter because the label is crowded with unskilled beginners; he uses a differentiating frame like a digital marketer specializing in done-for-you marketing systems.
cards.use_when: Writing your outreach bio, profile description or pitch line to a store or brand, and choosing how to describe what you do.
steps: Identify the label you'd default to and ask whether it is diluted in your niche — the source's example is copywriter, which he says many unskilled beginners claim.
Replace it with a frame describing outcome and mechanism: specializing in done-for-you email and marketing systems, or direct-response copywriting, rather than the generic role name.
Carry that frame consistently through your profile, videos and emails so the first impression is about capability, not category.
Use the frame as a differentiator the way a product uses a unique mechanism to stand out from an identical commodity.
caveats: This is the presenter's own positioning choice from his practice, not a rule; it works because he can back the frame with demos and past results.

cards.title: Rate and Scope Email Work by Sequencing a Client's Real Needs
cards.summary: When a prospect lists the flows they need, translate that list into a volume-and-price quote, treat a large project as a big-fish opportunity, and use fixed per-email pricing as the anchor.
cards.use_when: Quoting a store or brand that asks for multiple email flows — welcome/nurture, cart recovery, launch promotions, revival — as one engagement.
steps: Get the prospect to enumerate needs concretely: in the case study the client listed event ticket sales emails, an after-event upsell sequence, a welcome sequence for one audience, a nurture campaign for another, and a revival campaign for the existing database.
Count total units (the example totalled 50+ emails) so you can price by volume instead of guessing per project.
Quote a per-unit rate and, for genuinely large volumes, offer a volume discount — the case study went from $150/email to $100/email, presented as fair given the size.
If the total is rejected, split off a smaller sequence as the paid test (see the low-risk first-project approach).
When confirming scope in writing, restate exactly what is included so there is no ambiguity at delivery.
caveats: All figures are the presenter's own case-study pricing and not market benchmarks; the operative move is transparent volume-based pricing, not the specific rate.

cards.title: Warm Up Cold Outreach With Story Replies Before the Pitch
cards.summary: Reply to a prospect's story with a genuine, specific reaction, then wait a few days before sending the video intro and pitch — this softens the message and can prompt an invitation to pitch.
cards.use_when: Planning a multi-touch Instagram outreach sequence to a brand founder whose content you already follow.
steps: Reply to a recent piece of their content with something specific and sincere — the case replies were short lines like this is really smart marketing or I never thought about it that way before.
Let the reply sit for a couple of days rather than pitching straight away.
Follow with the video intro message that introduces you, what you do, and how you can help.

If they respond with openness, ask one diagnostic question about their setup — the case asked whether anyone on their team currently handles the marketing side — then follow up with a low-pressure call ask if no answer.
If they redirect you elsewhere (another person, email, an application form for a different role), keep the thread alive and re-anchor to the role you actually want.
caveats: The case study includes a $3k/month result and clients found this way, but that is one example, not a benchmark. Some prospects delegate DMs to salespeople, so be ready to be routed.

cards.title: Warm Handoff to Email: Be Ready With Sample Work and Portfolio
cards.summary: When a DM contact routes you to a manager or inbox, be prepared to hand over email samples and a portfolio immediately — that handoff is often what converts.
cards.use_when: You are doing social outreach to a brand and they ask you to email someone internally, or they request work samples.
steps: Expect the handoff: a reply like too busy, email this person is a path forward, not a rejection.
Have email samples ready to send the moment they ask so the conversation doesn't stall on your production time.
Maintain a portfolio link and be ready to say what other copy you write — in the case study the request was specifically for portfolio plus non-email copy types.
Offer to discuss small projects as the next step, framing it as seeing whether you're a good fit rather than pushing the biggest scope.
Expect practical steps like NDAs and briefs and keep moving — the same case closed a 10-email sequence at $2,000 with around 30–40 minutes of work per email.
caveats: The $2,000 / 10-email figure is a specific case study, not a rate card. The presenter also notes the buyer asked him to quote per email only after the deal was agreed — arrange pricing clarity earlier if you can.
